title: The Plateau Is the Lesson. What Sixty Flat Days Taught Me About Progress
body: Days forty to one hundred of learning the piano looked, from the outside, like nothing. The graph of my progress, if anyone had been cruel enough to plot it, was a flat line with a pulse. Same mistakes, same speed, same three pieces at the same stubborn level. I nearly quit on day sixty-one, and the quit that did not happen taught me more than the progress ever had. Here is what the plateau actually was, which took me sixty flat days to see. It was not absence of progress. It was progress changing its accounting. The first forty days had paid in visible coins. New notes, new chords, a piece getting faster. Around day forty the currency changed. The learning went underground, into consolidation, and consolidation pays nothing on screen. The fingers were not idle. They were doing the slow administrative work of making automatic what the mind had learned manually. Automatic is invisible while it builds. Then one day a passage that took conscious effort runs without you, and you think you improved that day. You improved on day fifty. The improvement was just clearing customs. The second thing the plateau was, was a measurement error. I was measuring the wrong thing. Speed, note accuracy, the three pieces. The skills that were actually growing, timing under pressure, hearing my own errors in real time, the tiny adjustments of wrist and shoulder, have no daily graph. They are measured in months, in whether the piece sounds like a person or like a caution. On day eighty-five someone said the new piece sounded relaxed. Relaxed. On the flat line, that word was a whole mountain range. The third thing, and the most uncomfortable, was that part of the plateau was my practice protecting itself. I was practicing what I could already do, because practicing what I could already do felt like progress and practicing what I could not do felt like drowning. The flat line was partly an honest plateau and partly a very busy comfort zone wearing practice clothes. The fix was specific. Twenty minutes of every session, no more, on the one passage I avoided. The passage I had been routing around like a pothole. Within two weeks the pothole was being paved, and the flat line, without fanfare, tilted. What finally moved the plateau was not intensity. It was a change of question. For sixty days the question had been, when will I be better. On day sixty-one, tired, I changed it to, what is better since day one. And the answer was embarrassing in its abundance. I could read the bass line without counting letters. My hands knew where middle C was in the dark. I could play the easy pieces while thinking about something else, which is a kind of literacy nobody notices getting, the way nobody notices getting fluent. The plateau is the lesson, and here is the form of the lesson. Progress in any real skill is not a ramp. It is stairs, and you live on the steps. The step is not the opposite of the climb. The step is where the climb gets installed. Every skill I have ever gained, I later found, had a sixty-day step in it somewhere, and the people who have the skill are simply the ones who kept showing up on the step, bored, unpaid, unphotographed, doing the consolidation work that no daily graph rewards. I am on a new plateau now, a different one, higher up, and I recognize it like an old hotel. Same furniture. Better view. I have a note above the piano that says only, you are on the stairs. It works on days when the flat line lies to me. The line is never flat. It is just drawing at a scale too honest for a Monday to appreciate.
